---
title: "Introduction to pySEB"
subtitle: "The ideas and vocabulary you need before writing code"
---

This tutorial assumes no experience with pySEB. It introduces the physical
question pySEB answers, the pieces used to describe a model, and the small
amount of vocabulary needed for the first executable tutorial.

You do not need to understand the full scattering theory before starting.
The [Theory Overview](https://github.com/Tobionecenobi/pySEB/wiki/Theory-Overview)
is available when you want the mathematical details.

## What problem does pySEB solve?

Small-angle scattering experiments measure how a sample scatters radiation as
a function of the magnitude of the scattering vector, $q$. Small q probes
large structural length scales; large q probes smaller details.

A model predicts a curve that can be compared with experimental data. pySEB
builds that prediction for structures assembled from connected components—for
example, two polymer blocks, chains attached to a particle, or a hierarchy of
repeated stars.

pySEB does not fit experimental data by itself. Its main job is to construct,
inspect, and evaluate the scattering model that a fitting workflow can use.

## The six ideas to know

| Idea | Plain-language meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subunit | One reusable scattering component | A solid sphere or Gaussian polymer |
| Reference point | A place or distribution through which subunits can connect | A sphere center, sphere surface, or polymer end |
| Link | A connection between two compatible references | Attach a polymer end to a sphere surface |
| Structure graph | The subunits and links forming one model | A diblock or micelle |
| Parameters | The physical values used when evaluating the graph | Radius, radius of gyration, and excess scattering length |
| q values | The reciprocal-length positions where the model is evaluated | Values in Å⁻¹ when lengths are in Å |

### Subunits

A subunit provides its own scattering equations and a set of named reference
points. `SolidSphere`, `GaussianPolymer`, and `ThinRod` are examples. A subunit
definition describes local physics; it does not decide what larger structure
the subunit belongs to.

### Fixed and distributed references

A fixed reference identifies one location, such as `center` or `end1`. A
distributed reference represents an average over a set of possible locations,
such as `surface` or `contour`.

This distinction matters. Attaching at a polymer end describes a different
ensemble from attaching at an independently sampled position along its
contour.

### A World and its graphs

A `World` is the workspace in which you add subunits, connect them, and name
complete structures. The topology is stored separately from the numerical
parameter values, so one graph can be evaluated repeatedly with different
sizes or contrasts.

## Read the smallest useful model

The next tutorial executes this pattern one step at a time:

```python
import pyseb

world = pyseb.World("FirstModel")
graph = world.Add("SolidSphere", "sphere")
world.Add(graph, "sphereModel")

parameters = {
    "beta_sphere": 1.0,
    "R_sphere": 50.0,
}

value = world.EvaluateFormFactor(
    "sphereModel", parameters, 0.01
)
print(value)
```

Line by line, this creates a workspace, adds one sphere instance, names the
complete graph, supplies its physical values, and evaluates its normalized
form factor at one q value.

## Parameter names

Generated parameter names combine a physical quantity with an instance name
or shared tag:

- `R_sphere` is the radius of the instance named `sphere`;
- `beta_sphere` is its excess scattering length;
- `Rg_chain` would be the radius of gyration shared by subunits tagged
  `chain`.

`beta` represents scattering contrast integrated over a subunit. It becomes
especially important when several subunits interfere or when contrast is
changed. Even when a normalized single-subunit curve does not visibly depend
on its magnitude, pySEB still uses the parameter consistently in composite
models.

## Units

pySEB does not impose a particular length unit on analytic calculations. It
requires consistency:

- if radii and lengths are in ångström, q must be in Å⁻¹;
- if radii and lengths are in nanometres, q must be in nm⁻¹.

Mixing the two shifts every feature of the predicted curve.

3. Choose a task from the [tutorial index](index.qmd).

After those first two models, terms such as `World`, subunit, link, reference,
